madagascar: Madagascar covers 592,800 square kilometres and is the world's fourth-largest island and second-largest island country. It split from Africa around 180 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent approximately 90 million years ago, so that its plants and animals evolved in relative isolation; over 90 per cent of its wildlife is endemic. A narrow, steep escarpment with tropical lowland forest runs along the east coast, and west of it lies a central plateau of terraced, rice-growing valleys between 750 and 1,500 metres high. The highest point is Maromokotro, at 2,876 metres.

Madagascar was first permanently settled during or before the mid-first millennium CE by Austronesian peoples, presumably arriving by outrigger canoe from present-day Indonesia, and scholars are cautious about dates earlier than 250 CE. The first settlers met giant lemurs, elephant birds and Malagasy hippopotamuses, which later became extinct through hunting and habitat destruction. Arab traders reached the island between the 7th and 9th centuries and brought Islam and the Arabic script, adapted as sorabe. Bantu-speaking migrants from south-eastern Africa arrived around the year 1000, and zebu cattle from South India were brought about then.

Until the late 18th century a fragmented set of shifting alliances ruled the island. King Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo as capital of the Imerina Kingdom around 1610 or 1625. From the early 19th century a series of Merina nobles united most of the island as the Kingdom of Madagascar. France's annexation ended the monarchy in 1897, and the country became independent in 1960.

Madagascar has had four republics and has been a constitutional democracy since 1992. A political crisis and coup in 2009 led to a long transition, and constitutional governance returned in January 2014. Malagasy and French are the official languages.

The Malagasy form over 90 per cent of the population, divided into 18 ethnic subgroups, of which the Merina of the highlands are the largest at about 26 per cent. The Malagasy language is of Malayo-Polynesian origin, closest to Ma'anyan of Borneo. The valiha, the most emblematic instrument, is a bamboo tube zither carried by early settlers from southern Borneo.
madrid: Madrid lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula on the southern Meseta Central, 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountain range, at an average altitude of about 650 metres. It straddles the Jarama and Manzanares river sub-drainage basins, within the wider catchment of the Tagus. The oldest urban core stands on hills beside the left bank of the Manzanares. The city grew eastwards to the creek now followed by the Paseo de la Castellana and on to the Abroñigal Creek, and also by annexing neighbouring settlements.

The origin of the name is unknown. Theories include a Latin derivation from matrix, a Celtic form meaning 'ford', and an Arabic word for a water stream, majrā. All have difficulty explaining the phonetic change fully. Nicknames include Los Madriles and La Villa y Corte, 'the town and court'.

The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. Archaeological remains include a settlement of the Celtic Carpetani, Roman villas, a Visigoth basilica near the church of Santa María de la Almudena and three Visigoth necropolises. The first historical document of an established settlement dates from the Muslim period. In the second half of the 9th century the Umayyad emir Muhammad I built a fortress on a headland near the Manzanares, one of many on the border between Al-Andalus and the kingdoms of León and Castile, to protect Toledo from attack from the north.

After the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in the early 11th century, Madrid became part of the Taifa of Toledo. In 1083 Alfonso VI of León and Castile seized it as an outpost against Toledo, which he took in 1085. Christians then occupied the centre of the town, while Muslims and Jews were displaced to the suburbs. Madrid remained a borderland for a time and suffered raids during the Almoravid period; its walls were destroyed in 1110. Philip II moved his court to Madrid in 1561 and transformed the town into a capital city.

Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain and of the autonomous community of Madrid, with about 3.4 million people in the city proper. Its landmarks include the Plaza Mayor, built in 1617 to 1619 and attributed to Juan Gómez de Mora, the Royal Palace, the Buen Retiro Park, founded in 1631, and the Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza museums along the Paseo del Prado, which form a UNESCO World Heritage site called the Golden Triangle of Art.
maeotians: The name comes from the sea: Maeotian was at first a label for the tribes living around the Maeotis, above all on its eastern coast. In sources of the 4th century BCE it has three senses: a broad term for the peoples around the sea, the name of the coastal tribes later listed by Strabo, and, in the usage of the Bosporan chancery, the lesser tribes of the Kuban region as distinct from the Sindi.

Their language, and even its family, is uncertain; the place names of their country suggest that they were not of Iranian stock. The Cambridge Ancient History reports two main views, that they were of Cimmerian ancestry, akin to the Thracians, or that they were Caucasian natives under Iranian overlordship. Soviet scholars concluded that they were among the ancestors of the Circassian, or Adyghe, people.

Strabo names among them the Sindi, Dandarii, Toreatae, Agri, Arrechi, Tarpetes, Obidiaceni, Sittaceni and Dosci, and adds that there were many others. Which peoples counted as Maeotian was disputed already in antiquity: Hellanicus of Lesbos and Pseudo-Scylax set the Sindi apart, while Pseudo-Scymnus and Strabo include them. The Sindi are the best attested and were probably the dominant people of the region.

The Maeotians lived in earthworks and open settlements on the Taman Peninsula and along the middle Kuban. According to Strabo they were as warlike as their nomadic neighbours, paid tribute at times to the rulers of Tanais and at times to the Bosporans, and rose in revolt from time to time. In the Kuban region they lived under successive steppe overlords. The graves show it: the ruling Scythians, and in Sindica the Sindian elite, were buried in richly furnished kurgans, while the Maeotian population used poorly equipped flat cemeteries.

In the early 4th century BCE Maeotian tribes fought a major war against the Bosporan Kingdom and its Sindian subjects. When the Sindian king Hecataeus repudiated his Maeotian wife Tirgatao, she roused her people, the Ixomatae, and other tribes to a destructive war on both kingdoms, which ended only under Gorgippus through supplication and gifts.

After Leucon I annexed Sindica, probably in the 380s BCE, the tribes of the Kuban were brought into the Bosporan state by stages. Leucon ruled the Toretae, Dandarii and Psessi as king, and under Paerisades I the royal style became king of the Sindi and all the Maeotians. Under Aspurgus, in the early 1st century CE, the royal titles still listed the Sindi and Maeotians, now with the Tarpetes and the people of Tanais.
mahapadma-nanda: What is told of Mahapadma comes from the Puranas, which make him the first Nanda king and the son of Mahanandin, the last king of the preceding Shaishunaga line, by a Shudra woman. His name, also given as Mahapadma-pati, means lord of the great lotus. Other traditions about the founder of the dynasty do not use this name at all.

Buddhist texts call the first Nanda king Ugrasena and describe him as of unknown lineage. According to the Mahavamsa-tika he came from the frontier region, was captured by a gang of robbers and later became their leader. One theory holds that Ugrasena was probably another name for Mahapadma. Jain texts such as the Parishishtaparvan and the Avashyaka sutra say that the Nanda king was the son of a courtesan by a barber and that he succeeded Udayin, with Kalpaka, a Jain, as his chief minister.

The Puranas describe him as ekarat, sole sovereign, and as sarva-kshatrantaka, destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, the warriors and rulers. The lines he is said to have exterminated include the Maithalas, Kasheyas, Ikshvakus, Panchalas, Shurasenas, Kurus, Haihayas, Vitihotras, Kalingas and Ashmakas.

The length of his reign is uncertain. The Matsya Purana assigns him 88 years, the Vayu Purana only 28. Modern estimates of his coronation also differ: the Indologist F. E. Pargiter put it in 382 BCE, the historian R. K. Mukherjee in 364 BCE and the historian H. C. Raychaudhuri about 345 BCE, and the beginning of Nanda rule has been placed as early as the 5th century BCE.

According to the Puranas, eight sons of Mahapadma ruled in succession after him for twelve years in all; only one, Sukalpa, is named. The Buddhist texts instead make the next eight kings brothers of the first, give the dynasty 22 years in total and name the last of them as Dhana Nanda.

Greek and Roman writers call the Nanda king of the time of Alexander's invasion Agrammes, possibly a corruption of the Sanskrit Augraseniya, son or descendant of Ugrasena. They suggest that the founder was a barber who took the throne from the last king of the earlier dynasty. The Roman historian Curtius, of the 1st century CE, reports on the authority of Porus that this barber became the queen's lover, murdered the king, seized power while pretending to act as guardian of the princes and later killed them, and that the king reigning in Alexander's day was his son.
mahatma-gandhi: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula and then part of a small princely state. His father Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi was the dewan, or chief minister, of Porbandar and later of Rajkot. A family friend advised that he study law in London, and to win his mother's consent he vowed to abstain from meat, alcohol and women. The elders of the Modh Bania community excommunicated him from his caste, but he sailed on 4 September 1888 and was called to the bar at 22.

After two uncertain years in India, Gandhi went to South Africa in April 1893 to represent an Indian merchant in a lawsuit, and stayed for 21 years. He faced discrimination at once: he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave the first-class compartment. He had thought of himself as a Briton first and an Indian second, but the prejudice he saw made him question his people's standing in the British Empire. There he first used nonviolent resistance, in a campaign for civil rights.

Gandhi returned to India in 1915 at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He took leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1920 and formulated satyagraha as a political movement in a Resolution on Non-cooperation that September. Congress declared the independence of India on 26 January 1930, and that year he led the 400 km Dandi Salt March against the British salt tax. In 1942 he demanded immediate independence, and the British imprisoned him and tens of thousands of Congress leaders. He was imprisoned many times in both South Africa and India.

The Muslim League moved, against Gandhi's strong opposition, to demand a separate Muslim state. In August 1947 the British partitioned the land, and India and Pakistan each became independent on terms Gandhi disapproved. Religious violence followed, especially in Punjab and Bengal. He visited the affected areas and undertook several hunger strikes to stop the violence.

On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who opposed Gandhi's advocacy of nonviolence and his friendship with Indian Muslims, shot him three times in the chest in the garden of Birla House in Delhi on his way to a prayer meeting. Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, Gandhi Jayanti, and is marked worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence. He is regarded as the Father of the Nation in India and was often called Bapu. His pamphlet Hind Swaraj of 1909 became the intellectual blueprint of the independence movement. Writers differ on him, some presenting a paragon of ethical living and others a more complex, contradictory and changing figure.
maize: Maize, Zea mays, is a tall annual grass with a single stem, ranging in height from 1.2 to 4 m. The tassel at the top bears the male flowers, and a female inflorescence lower down develops into an ear wrapped in husks. The grains are usually yellow or white in modern varieties but can be orange, red, brown, blue, purple or black. Maize relies on humans for its propagation, since its kernels, unlike those of its wild ancestor teosinte, do not fall off the cob on their own.

The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov in 1931 and by George Beadle in 1932. In 2004 John Doebley identified Balsas teosinte, native to the Balsas River valley in Mexico's south-western highlands, as the wild relative most similar to maize. All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700-year-old layer in a cave near Iguala, Guerrero, and maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8,000 years ago.
The Olmec and Maya cultivated it in numerous varieties and processed it by nixtamalization, and by 3,000 years ago it was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language and myths.

The niacin in maize is not available without nixtamalization, the alkali treatment, and the Maya made nixtamal meal into porridges and tamales. After 1492 explorers and traders carried maize to Europe. Spanish settlers preferred wheat bread, and maize flour could not replace wheat in communion bread, since only wheat was believed able to undergo transubstantiation. Maize was nevertheless grown in Spain within a few decades of Columbus's voyages, and by the 18th century it was the chief food of the southern French and Italian peasantry, especially as polenta.
majeerteen: The Majeerteen, also known as Mohammed Harti, belong to the Harti branch of the Darod. They traditionally inhabit the Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions, from Bosaso to Garacad, between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and are most numerous in the regional capitals of Bosaso, Garowe and Galkacyo. Migrations that began in the 19th century took some to Kismayo in the south, and some live in the Dollo Zone of the Somali Region of Ethiopia. Historically the clan formed part of a coastal trading network around the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

The first recorded mention of the clan in English is by Henry Salt, who described them as living on the coast of Hafun under a Sultan Hassan. Salt relates that the Imam of Muscat had sent gifts and asked leave to build a small fort there, and that both the request and the gifts were refused. In the 19th century Majeerteen merchants were active across the Red Sea. One of them, Ahmed Muhammad, was granted the island of Baka by the Damoheita Afar, and his family ruled it as sultans into the period of Italian rule in Eritrea.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the 15th or 16th century and rose to prominence in the 19th under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. It was nearly destroyed by his struggle with his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid, who was forced into exile in Yemen, returned with a band of Hadhrami musketeers, overpowered the local Hawiye clans and founded the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

Kenadid signed a protectorate treaty with Italy, and Boqor Osman followed in late 1889. Each hoped to use Italian support against the other and to avoid direct occupation. When Kenadid refused to let British troops land in his territory to fight the Dervish forces of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the Italians exiled him to Aden and then to Eritrea. After two years of resistance by Boqor Osman and Majeerteen rebels, which Italian forces put down with long coastal bombardments of towns and naval blockades, the territory came under the full authority of Rome by late 1927.

Osman Yusuf Kenadid, a son of the first sultan of Hobyo, devised the Osmanya script for the Somali language in the 1920s. Members of the clan held many government posts in the 1960s and 1970s, among them Abdirashid Shermarke, the first prime minister and second president of Somalia. In the 1980s and 1990s the Somali Salvation Democratic Front was a predominantly Majeerteen political group.
malawi: Malawi is a landlocked country in Southeast Africa, bordered by Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique. The Great Rift Valley runs through it from north to south, and Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, makes up over three-quarters of its eastern boundary. The lake is about 587 kilometres long and 84 kilometres wide, and the Shire River flows from its southern end to join the Zambezi in Mozambique. South of the lake lie the Shire Highlands, where the Zomba and Mulanje peaks rise. The altitude moderates what would otherwise be an equatorial climate, with rains between November and April.

The name Malawi means 'flames' in Chichewa and Chitumbuka and was chosen by the first president, Hastings Banda, after independence in 1964. It comes from the Maravi, a Bantu ethnic group that emigrated from the southern Congo around 1400.

Before the arrival of Bantu peoples from the north around the 10th century CE, the area had a small population of hunter-gatherers, known in oral tradition as Akafula or BaTwa, who were gradually overtaken by agrarian Bantu peoples. By the 16th century the Bantu groups had established kingdoms such as the Maravi Empire, which reached from north of Nkhotakota to the Zambezi River, and the Nkhamanga. In the 17th century, with the area mostly united under one ruler, people began trading and making alliances with Portuguese traders and soldiers. By the 18th century the empire had broken up.

The Indian Ocean slave trade reached its height in the mid-19th century, when about 20,000 people a year are believed to have been enslaved and taken from Nkhotakota to Kilwa. David Livingstone reached Lake Malawi in 1859 and identified the Shire Highlands as suitable for European settlement.

Anglican and Presbyterian missions followed Livingstone's visit in the 1860s and 1870s, the African Lakes Company was established in 1878, and a British consul took up residence at Blantyre in 1883. To prevent Portuguese occupation, the British government sent Harry Johnston as consul to make treaties with local rulers. In 1891 the area became the British Central African Protectorate, renamed Nyasaland in 1907. Nyasaland became independent under Hastings Banda in 1964.

Malawi is the Republic of Malawi, with its capital and largest city at Lilongwe and its commercial centre at Blantyre. English is the official language, and Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Chiyao are major regional languages. Lake Malawi National Park, listed in 1984, and the Chongoni Rock Art Area, listed in 2006, are its two UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
mali: Mali is a landlocked country of 1,240,192 square kilometres in West Africa, the eighth largest in Africa. Its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara Desert, and most of the country lies in the southern Sahara, while southern Mali, where the majority of inhabitants live, is in the Sudanian savanna. The Niger and Senegal rivers run through the south. Late April to early October is the rainy season there, and flooding of the Niger is common, creating the Inner Niger Delta. The Adrar des Ifoghas massif lies in the northeast, and gold, uranium, phosphates, salt and limestone are among its natural resources.

Rock art in the Sahara suggests that northern Mali has been inhabited since about 10,000 BCE, when the Sahara was fertile. Early ceramics from Ounjougou, dating to about 9,400 BCE, are believed to show an independent invention of pottery. Farming took place by 5000 BCE and iron was used by around 500 BCE. In the first millennium BCE Mandé peoples related to the Soninke created early towns along the middle Niger, among them Dia, from around 900 BCE, and Djenné-Djenno, which lasted from around 300 BCE to 900 CE.

Mali was part of three successive West African empires that controlled this trade: the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire. At its peak in 1300 the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa, and Mansa Musa is believed to have been one of the wealthiest individuals in history. Medieval Mali was a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge, and Timbuktu became a notable place of education.

The Songhai Empire absorbed the Mali Empire in 1468, and a Saadian army defeated the Songhai in 1591. In the late 19th century France seized control during the Scramble for Africa and made it part of French Sudan. It became independent in 1960, first in a brief federation with Senegal, and then as the Republic of Mali.

Bamako is the capital and largest city. The name Mali comes from the Mali Empire and originally meant hippopotamus, the clan symbol of the Keita dynasty. Most people live in the south, and the Bambara are the largest ethnic group, with the Fulani, Senufo, Malinke, Soninke, Dogon, Songhai and Tuareg among others. Malian musical tradition derives from the griots, the Keepers of Memories, and literary tradition is passed mainly by word of mouth, with jalis reciting histories and stories known by heart.
malta: Malta is an archipelago in the central Mediterranean, about 80 kilometres from southern Italy across the Malta Channel. Only Malta, Gozo and Comino have permanent residents, and Comino is practically uninhabited. The islands lie on a shallow shelf that was once part of a land bridge between Sicily and North Africa, and the archipelago sits on the African tectonic plate. The terrain is coarse and hilly, with many harbours along an indented coastline. The highest point, Ta' Dmejrek near Dingli, is 253 metres high, and Malta has no rivers or lakes.

The earliest reliable evidence of habitation dates to 6500 BCE, when Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, probably from Sicily, arrived. Neolithic farmers from Sicily are thought to have followed by around 5400 BCE. Around 3500 BCE the islanders built the Ġgantija temples on Gozo, among the oldest free-standing structures in the world, and other early temples include those at Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra. After 2500 BCE Malta was depopulated until a new people arrived who cremated their dead and built small dolmens as tombs; they probably differed from the temple builders.

Phoenician traders colonised the islands around 1000 BCE, with their seat of government at Mdina and their main port at Cospicua on the Grand Harbour, which they called Maleth. Carthage controlled the islands after the fall of Phoenicia. It is unsure whether Roman rule began after the first or second Punic War, but Rome held Malta after the second, when it was surrendered by Hamilcar, a son of Gisco, to the consul Titus Sempronius Longus. The Arabs, Normans and Aragonese ruled in the Middle Ages, and the Knights Hospitaller, French and British in the modern era.

Malta became a British crown colony in the early 19th century and served as headquarters of the British Mediterranean Fleet. It was besieged by the Axis powers in the Second World War. Independence came in 1964, and the current parliamentary republic was established in 1974. Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and the eurozone on 1 January 2008.

The two official languages are Maltese, a Semitic language with close ties to Arabic and Sicilian, and English. Catholicism is the state religion, though the constitution guarantees freedom of religion. The 2025 census counted 588,254 people.
manas-river: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.
manghud: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.

In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.
mark-twain: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on 30 November 1835 in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children of Jane Lampton, a native of Kentucky, and John Marshall Clemens, a lawyer from Virginia. Only three of his siblings lived beyond childhood. When he was four the family moved to Hannibal, Missouri, a port town on the Mississippi River that inspired the fictional St. Petersburg of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. Slavery was legal in Missouri at the time and became a theme in those books.

Twain became a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi, which gave him the material for Life on the Mississippi (1883). He then went west to join Orion in Nevada, joked about his failure at mining, and turned to journalism for the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise. A humorous story about a jumping frog of Calaveras County, published in 1865 and based on a tale he heard at the Angels Hotel in Angels Camp, California, brought him international attention. He became a much sought-after speaker.

His novels include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), and he wrote The Gilded Age (1873) with Charles Dudley Warner. He began with light humorous verse and became a chronicler of the vanities, hypocrisies and murderous acts of mankind. In Huckleberry Finn he combined humor, narrative and social criticism, and he helped create a distinctive American literature built on American themes and language. The book has been repeatedly restricted in American high schools, not least for its frequent use of a racial slur.

His pen name, he said, came from the riverboatman's cry of mark twain, meaning that the water was two fathoms deep. He also said he took it from Captain Isaiah Sellers, who signed river news with it for the New Orleans Picayune. Some have doubted this story. His views became more radical with age, and he supported the labor movement, among others the Knights of Labor. He died of a heart attack on 21 April 1910, the day after Halley's Comet was closest to the Sun, as he had predicted.
martin-luther: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 to Hans Luder and his wife Margarethe in Eisleben. In 1484 the family moved to Mansfeld, where his father leased copper mines and smelters and later became a town councillor. Hans was determined that his eldest son should become a lawyer. Luther entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and received his master's degree in 1505, but dropped out of law almost at once. According to one story, a lightning bolt struck near him during a thunderstorm on 2 July 1505, and he cried out, "Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!" He entered St Augustine's Monastery in Erfurt on 17 July 1505, to his father's fury.

As an Augustinian friar Luther devoted himself to fasting, prayer and confession, and described this period as one of deep spiritual despair. He was ordained on 3 April 1507, began teaching theology at the University of Wittenberg in 1508 and received his Doctor of Theology on 19 October 1512, succeeding Johann von Staupitz as chair of theology.

From 1510 to 1520 he lectured on the Psalms, Hebrews, Romans and Galatians, and became convinced that the Church was corrupt. The most important doctrine for him was justification by faith alone through God's grace, which he held to be entirely God's work. He taught that the Bible is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge of the Gospel, which challenged the authority of the pope and bishops. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521, and that year Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms.

At Luther's death in 1546 his excommunication was still in effect. He made effective use of the printing press and wrote in German to reach a broader audience; between 1500 and 1530 his works made up one fifth of all materials printed in Germany. His German Bible of 1534 fostered a standard version of the German language, and his marriage to Katharina von Bora, a former nun, set a model for clerical marriage.

Luther expressed staunchly antisemitic views, calling for the expulsion of Jews and the burning of synagogues. According to the prevailing opinion among historians, his anti-Jewish rhetoric contributed significantly to the development of antisemitism in Germany, and Nazi propaganda cited it.
martin-luther-king-jr: Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. on 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, the second of three children of Michael King and Alberta King. His maternal grandfather, Adam Daniel Williams, was a minister who became pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church. King enrolled at Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania, where he was elected president of the student body, and later studied at Boston University. He married Coretta Scott on 18 June 1953.

King oversaw the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott, was the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, helped organise the 1963 protests in Birmingham, Alabama, and was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave the I Have a Dream speech. On 14 October 1964 he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. The FBI director J. Edgar Hoover ordered surveillance of him, and a 1975 congressional investigation found that from December 1963 until his death he was the target of an intensive campaign to neutralise him.

In March 1968 King went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support striking black sanitation workers, and on 3 April gave the address I've Been to the Mountaintop. He was assassinated on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray was convicted of the killing, though conspiracy theories persist, and King's death led to riots in American cities. Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed as a federal holiday in 1986.
mattavilasa-prahasana: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.
mauritania: Mauritania lies in the western region of Africa and is generally flat, its 1,030,000 square kilometres forming vast, arid plains broken by occasional ridges and clifflike outcroppings. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Senegal, Mali, Algeria and Western Sahara, and is considered part of both the Sahel and the Maghreb. Approximately three-quarters of the country is desert or semidesert, and the desert has been expanding since the mid-1960s after extended, severe drought. The highest of its sandstone plateaus, the Adrar Plateau, reaches 500 metres, and the concentric Guelb er Richat is a prominent feature of the north-central region.

The name comes from Mauretania, the Latin name of an ancient Berber kingdom and later Roman province that lay considerably farther north, along the western Mediterranean coast of Africa. The territories do not overlap. Arab geographers more commonly called the land Bilad Chinqit, the land of Chinguetti. The French officially used the term Mauritanie occidentale in 1899, on a proposal by the colonial administrator Xavier Coppolani.

The ancient tribes of Mauritania were the Niger-Congo and Bafour peoples. The Bafour were among the first Saharan peoples to abandon a nomadic lifestyle for agriculture, and migrated southward as the Sahara dried. They were displaced by Berbers who arrived between the 3rd and 7th centuries. The Umayyads were the first Arab Muslims to enter the region, establishing themselves by the end of the 7th century. In the 11th century several Berber confederations in the desert joined to form the Almoravid movement, which built an empire stretching from the Sahara to the Iberian Peninsula.

From 1644 to 1674 the indigenous peoples made a final, unsuccessful effort to repel the Maqil Arabs, led by the Beni Hassan tribe, in the Char Bouba War. The descendants of the Beni Hassan warriors became the upper stratum of Moorish society, and Hassaniya, a bedouin Arabic dialect named for them, became the dominant language of the largely nomadic population. In the early 20th century France colonised the country as part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960.

Mauritania is the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. Its capital and largest city is Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast, and its population is about 5 million. Arabic is the official language, with Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages, and Islam is the state religion. Its manuscript libraries at Chinguetti hold thousands of medieval manuscripts, and it has a long oral tradition of poetry.
mauritius: The main island lies 1,100 nautical miles (2,000 km) off the southeast coast of Africa, between latitudes 19°58.8'S and 20°31.7'S. It is 65 km long and 45 km wide. It is geologically young, created by volcanic activity some 8 million years ago, and with Réunion, Rodrigues and Saint Brandon it forms part of the Mascarene Islands, which are no longer volcanically active. White sandy beaches surround it, and lagoons are protected by a coral reef. The country also includes Rodrigues, Agaléga and St. Brandon. The main island was the only known home of the dodo, which became extinct soon after human settlement.

The island was uninhabited when first visited. Some historians have speculated from the Cantino planisphere of 1502, where it appears as Dina Arobi, that Arab sailors reached it around 975. Portuguese sailors visited in 1507, and Diogo Fernandes Pereira is the first European known to have landed; the Portuguese did not stay. A Dutch squadron under Admiral Wybrand Van Warwyck landed at Grand Port in 1598 and named the island after Prince Maurice of Nassau. The Dutch inhabited it from 1638, exploiting ebony trees and introducing sugar cane, domestic animals and deer.

French colonisation began in 1715, and the island was renamed Isle de France. In 1810 the United Kingdom seized it, and France ceded Mauritius and its dependencies in the Treaty of Paris. The British colony included Rodrigues, Agaléga, St. Brandon, the Chagos Archipelago and, until 1906, the Seychelles. Mauritius became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony and stayed a plantation colony dominated by sugar until independence in 1968. The country became a republic in 1992.

In 1965, three years before independence, the United Kingdom split the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius to form the British Indian Ocean Territory, established on 8 November 1965. The local population was forcibly expelled, and the main island, Diego Garcia, was leased to the United States for a military base.

Mauritius is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral National Assembly, and its capital and largest city is Port Louis. Its people are diverse in ethnicity, culture, language and faith, drawn from Indian, African, Chinese and European, mostly French, origins. It is the only country in Africa where Hinduism is the most practised religion. Its architecture combines Dutch, French and British styles with influences from India and East Africa.
may-coup-poland: Józef Piłsudski had largely controlled the politics of the re-established Polish state but lost that advantage after the failed Kiev offensive of spring 1920, while keeping the esteem of parts of the armed forces. In November 1925 the cabinet of Władysław Grabski gave way to that of Aleksander Skrzyński, backed by the National Democrats and the Polish Socialist Party; when the socialists withdrew, it fell in turn and was replaced by a government under Wincenty Witos, formed by the Polish People's Party "Piast" and the Christian Union of National Unity. It had even less popular support than its predecessors.

Piłsudski regarded the constant shifts of power in the Sejm, the Polish parliament, as chaotic and damaging. He also saw threats to Poland's independence in the Locarno Treaties of 1925, by which the western but not the eastern borders of Germany were guaranteed, and in the Treaty of Berlin concluded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1926.

On 10 May 1926, the day the Witos government was formed, Piłsudski told the newspaper Kurier Poranny that he was ready to fight the evil of sejmocracy, a contemptuous word for rule by parliament, and promised a sanation, or restoration to health, of political life. The edition was confiscated. In the night of 11–12 May units of the Warsaw garrison marched to Rembertów and pledged him their support; on 12 May they moved on Warsaw and took the bridges over the Vistula River.

At about 17:00 Piłsudski met President Stanisław Wojciechowski on the Poniatowski Bridge. He demanded the resignation of the cabinet; the president demanded that his forces capitulate. Fighting began at about 19:00. On 14 May the Polish Socialist Party declared for the rebels and called a general strike, and striking railwaymen kept government reinforcements from reaching Warsaw. To prevent a nationwide civil war, Wojciechowski and Witos resigned. In all 215 soldiers and 164 civilians were killed and some 900 people wounded.

Kazimierz Bartel formed a new government with Piłsudski as minister of military affairs. On 31 May the National Assembly nominated Piłsudski as president, but he declined, and Ignacy Mościcki took the office. Piłsudski held the posts of defence minister and inspector general of the armed forces in every government until his death, and headed two of them himself, in 1926–1928 and 1930. In 1935 his supporters replaced the democratic March Constitution with the April Constitution, which provided for a strong presidency but came too late for him to assume it.
mediterranean: The Mediterranean Sea is an intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia and Africa, almost completely enclosed by land. It connects to the Atlantic Ocean by the Strait of Gibraltar, only 14 km wide, to the Black Sea by the Bosporus, and to the Red Sea by the Suez Canal. It covers about 2,500,000 km2 and has fifteen marginal seas, among them the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Marmara. Its average depth is 1,500 m, and the deepest point, 5,109 m, lies in the Calypso Deep in the Ionian Sea. The Nile is the longest river to end in it. Sicily and Sardinia are its two largest islands.

Geological evidence indicates that around 5.9 million years ago the sea was cut off from the Atlantic and was partly or completely dried up over some 600,000 years, in the Messinian salinity crisis. It was refilled about 5.3 million years ago by the Zanclean flood, in less than two years according to scientists' estimates.

The Levant, in the eastern Mediterranean, was among the first regions in the world with permanent human habitation, as early as 12,000 BCE. The earliest advanced civilisations on the sea were the Egyptians and the Minoans, who traded extensively with each other. Around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age Collapse destroyed many cities and trade routes in the east. The Greek city-states and the Phoenicians later colonised its coastlines extensively. Darius I of Persia, who conquered Egypt, built a canal linking the Red Sea to the Nile and so to the Mediterranean, wide enough for two triremes to pass and needing four days to traverse.

After the Punic Wars of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE the Roman Republic defeated the Carthaginians and became the preeminent power in the western Mediterranean. Once Augustus founded the Roman Empire, the Romans called it Mare Nostrum, Our Sea. For the next 400 years the empire controlled the sea and virtually all its coasts from Gibraltar to the Levant, which earned it the nickname Roman Lake. Rome is the only state to have ever controlled all of its coasts.

The Romans also called the sea Mare Magnum and Mare Internum. The name Mare Mediterraneum, meaning in the middle of land, is first attested in the 6th century in the work of Isidore of Seville. Arabic writers called it the Sea of the Romans, and the Ancient Egyptians called it Wadj-wr, great green. The countries on its shores include Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt and Morocco, and Cyprus and Malta are island countries within it. Its mild winters and warm summers give their name to the Mediterranean climate type.
megali-idea: The expression first appeared in the debates between Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis and King Otto that preceded the constitution of 1844, but the hope behind it was older. Greeks had long looked for liberation from Ottoman rule and a restoration of the Byzantine Empire; folklore told that the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, had been turned to marble and lay beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople awaiting the call to reconquer the city. The state created in 1830 was designed by the Great Powers, and most ethnic Greeks still lived outside it, within the Ottoman Empire.

The new state was imagined as the Greece of Two Continents and Five Seas, reaching from the Ionian Sea to Anatolia and the Black Sea and from Thrace, Macedonia and Epirus to Crete and Cyprus. When the Danish prince Wilhelm Georg was elected king in 1863 he was styled King of the Hellenes rather than King of Greece, implying a king of all Greeks wherever they lived.

The Ionian Islands were acquired in 1864. In 1897, with violence growing in Crete, a Greek force of 1,500 men under Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed at Kolymbari on 1 February and proclaimed the island's union with Greece. Irregulars then raided Turkish outposts in Thessaly without orders, and the Ottoman Empire declared war. The Greek army fell back, an armistice was signed in May, and Greece lost small border territories and paid reparations; Crete became an autonomous state with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.

Eleftherios Venizelos, a Cretan who became prime minister after the Goudi coup of 1909, was a major proponent of the idea, and under him Greek territory doubled in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13. Greece joined the Allies in 1917 and afterwards gained a protectorate over Smyrna and its hinterland, where a referendum was to follow five years of Greek administration, and a frontier in Thrace a few miles from the walls of Constantinople.

Turkish revolutionaries defeated the Greek army and expelled the Greeks from Anatolia. By the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece ceded Eastern Thrace, Imbros, Tenedos and Smyrna. During the conflict 151,892 Greeks had already fled Asia Minor; the treaty moved 1,104,216 Greeks from Turkey, while 380,000 Turks left Greece. The League of Nations arranged a loan of 150 million francs to help settle the refugees. In 1930 Venizelos paid an official visit to Turkey, where he proposed Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The Dodecanese were acquired after the Second World War, in 1947.
mexico: Mexico covers 1,972,550 square kilometres, the thirteenth-largest country in the world, with coastlines on the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. The central and northern territories lie at high altitudes. The highest elevations are in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which includes Pico de Orizaba at 5,700 metres and Popocatépetl at 5,462 metres, and the Sierra Madre Oriental and Sierra Madre Occidental cross the country from north to south. The Chicxulub crater lies on the Yucatán peninsula, and much of the land mass is unsuited to agriculture because of aridity, soil or terrain.

Human presence dates back to at least 11,500 BCE, although dates as old as 28,000 BCE have been proposed for less securely dated sites. Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato and beans, which allowed sedentary agricultural villages to begin around 5000 BCE.

The Olmec culture, the earliest complex civilization, flourished on the Gulf Coast from around 1500 BCE, and the Maya and Zapotec civilizations later developed complex centres. Teotihuacán, with a population of more than 150,000, formed a military and commercial empire, and after its collapse around 600 CE other centres competed. Toward the end of the post-Classic period the Aztecs established an empire based in Tenochtitlan.

Spanish colonization began in 1521 with an indigenous alliance that defeated the Aztec Empire, establishing the colony of New Spain. The Mexican War of Independence of 1810 to 1821 ended Peninsular rule. In 1848 Mexico lost nearly half its territory in the Mexican–American War. Liberal reforms in the Constitution of 1857 led to civil war and French intervention, and the Second Mexican Empire under Emperor Maximilian I of Habsburg was overthrown by Republican forces led by Benito Juárez. The long rule of Porfirio Díaz ended with the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, which brought the Constitution of 1917, the current one.

Mexico has about 131 million inhabitants, and Mexico City is the capital and largest city. It is a federal republic with a presidential system and 32 states, with a bicameral Congress of the Union of 500 deputies and 128 senators. The Constitution gives Spanish legal equality with 68 indigenous languages.
mexico-city: Mexico City lies in the Valley of Mexico, also called the Basin of Mexico, in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt on the high plateaus of south-central Mexico. Its lowest point is about 2,200 metres above sea level, and mountains and volcanoes of over 5,000 metres surround it. The valley has no natural drainage outlet for the water that runs down from the slopes, so the city has long been open to flooding.

The Mexica founded Mexico-Tenochtitlan in 1325 or 1327 on an island in the lake system, which it shared with a smaller city-state, Tlatelolco. According to legend, the god Huitzilopochtli showed them the site by presenting a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear and devouring a rattlesnake. Between 1325 and 1521 the city came to dominate the other city-states round Lake Texcoco, and the Aztec Empire reached both the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific.

Hernán Cortés, with the aid of many other native peoples, reached Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519 and was greeted by the ruler Moctezuma II, whom he then placed under house arrest. After the siege of 1521 the city was nearly destroyed and was rebuilt to Spanish urban standards. The municipality of México Tenochtitlán was established in 1524, and from 1585 the city was officially Ciudad de México. It was a major political, administrative and financial centre of the colonial period.

After independence, the Federal Constitution of 4 October 1824 let Congress choose the seat of the federal government. Mexico City was preferred to Querétaro, largely through the persuasion of Servando Teresa de Mier, as the centre of the country's population and history. The choice was made official on 18 November 1824, and a surface of two leagues square centred on the Zocalo was separated from the State of Mexico as the Federal District. Residents won the right to elect their head of government in 1997, and on 29 January 2016 the district was renamed Ciudad de México.

Mexico City is the capital and largest city of Mexico, divided into 16 boroughs, or alcaldías. The 2020 census gave the city proper 9,209,944 people, and Greater Mexico City 21,804,515. Its historic centre and the muralist works of José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros and Diego Rivera, at the National Palace and the Palacio de Bellas Artes among other buildings, belong to the heritage of the Mexican capital.
micaela-bastidas: Micaela Bastidas was born on 23 June 1744, the natural daughter of Josefa Puyucahua Sisa and Manuel Bastidas, who died in 1746. Virtually nothing is known of her father, who was perhaps a priest or of African descent; some documents call her a zamba, the colonial term for a person of mixed African and indigenous ancestry, while her marriage certificate lists both parents as Spaniards, a label that may have been a sign of respectability. As an illegitimate child she was marginalised in the overwhelmingly indigenous highlands. She spoke Quechua better than Spanish, was a devout Catholic and had little formal schooling.

She married on 25 May 1760, before her sixteenth birthday, in the church of Our Lady of Purification in Surimana. Her husband, a descendant of the Inca Túpac Amaru I, was named cacique of Pampamarca, Tungasuca and Surimana in 1764 and traded across a wide network with 350 mules. They lived in Tinta and had three sons, Hipólito, Mariano and Fernando. Letters exchanged early in the rebellion show endearments and concern for each other's safety.

The rebellion opened on 4 November 1780, when the local Spanish commander Antonio de Arriaga was taken prisoner; he was later hanged. The rebels made their headquarters at Tungasuca and defeated the Spanish at Sangarará on 18 November. Because indigenous people were forbidden firearms, obtaining weapons was among the hardest of her tasks. She also issued safe-conducts, took charge of the rearguard, guarded against espionage and organised a service of mounted chasquis that carried messages across rebel territory.

Local rulers called her Señora Gobernadora, La Coya or La Reina, and one description calls her a superior strategist to her husband and certainly more daring. He held off from Cuzco, which allowed the Spaniards to bring in reinforcements. By March 1781 the rebel army numbered seven thousand men and women.

On 18 May 1781 the prisoners were taken to be executed. Hipólito had his tongue cut out and was hanged. Micaela Bastidas fought her executioners until they subdued her and cut off her tongue. A hand-cranked garrote made for the occasion could not be used because her neck was so slender, and she was strangled with a rope, beaten with a club and kicked to death, in front of her husband, who was then killed. Their bodies were dismembered and the parts sent to towns of the region for display. The involvement of women in such risings shocked the Spanish authorities, who gave them the same penalties as men.
michelangelo: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was born on 6 March 1475 in Caprese, near Arezzo in Tuscany, where his father Ludovico was the town's judicial administrator. The family had for generations been small-scale bankers in Florence, but the bank failed. Several months after his birth they returned to Florence. After his mother's death in 1481 he lived with a nanny and her husband, a stonecutter, in Settignano, where his father owned a marble quarry and a small farm. He later said he received the knack of handling chisel and hammer with the milk of his nurse.

Michelangelo achieved fame early, and two of his best-known works, the Pietà and David, were sculpted before he was 30. Born in the Republic of Florence, he was mostly active in Rome from his thirties onward. Although he did not consider himself a painter, he created the scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and The Last Judgment on its altar wall, two of the most influential frescoes in Western art.

His design of the Laurentian Library pioneered Mannerist architecture. At 71 he succeeded Antonio da Sangallo the Younger as architect of St. Peter's Basilica, and he changed the plan so that the western end was finished to his design, as was the dome, with some modification after his death on 18 February 1564. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime: Giorgio Vasari's Lives of 1550 called him divino, and Ascanio Condivi's Life of 1553 was prepared with his participation.

The Madonna of the Stairs is his earliest known work in marble, carved in shallow relief. His Bacchus, a commission with a set subject, has the traditional wine cup, vine wreath and fawn, but shows the god with bleary eyes and an unsteady stance. In the Madonna of Bruges the Christ Child, held by his mother's hand, is about to step off into the world. His contemporaries admired his terribilità, the ability to instil awe in those who saw his art.

He wrote more than three hundred sonnets and madrigals. He was a devout Catholic whose faith deepened at the end of his life. Attempts by later artists to imitate the expressive physicality of his style helped bring about Mannerism. The dome of St. Peter's influenced church building for centuries, including St Paul's Cathedral in London, and his unfinished giants for the tomb of Pope Julius II had a deep effect on sculptors such as Rodin and Henry Moore.
miguel-de-cervantes: Many details of Cervantes's life remain uncertain, including his name, background and appearance. He signed his name as Cerbantes, but his printers used Cervantes, which became the common form. In later life he used Saavedra, the name of a distant relative, rather than Cortinas, after his mother. It is generally accepted that he was born around 29 September 1547 in Alcalá de Henares, the second son of the barber-surgeon Rodrigo de Cervantes and Leonor de Cortinas.

Rodrigo was often in debt or looking for work, and the family moved constantly. When he was imprisoned for debt from October 1553 to April 1554, Leonor supported the family alone. They lived in Córdoba until 1556, when his grandfather died. It has been suggested that one or both parents were New Christians, Catholics of Jewish ancestry, but the view has no wide following. No authenticated portrait of Cervantes is known to exist.

In 1569 Cervantes was forced to leave Spain and went to Rome, where he worked in a cardinal's household. In 1570 he enlisted in a Spanish Navy infantry regiment. He was badly wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571. Captured by Barbary pirates in 1575 while serving as a soldier, he was ransomed after five years and returned to Madrid.

He claimed to have written more than 20 plays, such as El trato de Argel, based on his captivity, but such works were short-lived. His first significant novel, the pastoral romance La Galatea, appeared in 1585 and received little notice. He worked as a purchasing agent and later as a government tax collector. By 1605 he had not been published for 20 years.

Don Quixote, first published in January 1605, set out explicitly to undermine vain and empty chivalric romances. Its portrayal of real life and its everyday speech were considered innovative, and it was instantly popular: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza appeared in masquerades celebrating the birth of Philip IV on 8 April 1605. An unauthorised sequel under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda came out in 1614, and Cervantes published his own second part in 1615. The first part is more comic, the second more sophisticated, with greater depth of characterisation.

His other works include the twelve Novelas ejemplares of 1613, the allegorical poem Viaje del Parnaso, eight short farces, and Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda, published after his death in 1617. English writers rediscovered him in the mid-18th century, and John Bowle published an annotated edition of Don Quixote in 1781. It has been translated into all major languages.
mir-osman-ali-khan: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.
moamoria-rebellion: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.
mohamed-amin-didi: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.
moldova: Moldova is a landlocked country of 33,843 km2 between the Prut river on the west, which separates it from Romania, and the Dniester on the east. Most of it is hilly, with elevations that never exceed 430 metres, the highest point being the Bălănești Hill, and exceptionally rich Chernozem soil covers around three-quarters of the land. About 88% of the area lies in the Bessarabia region, and a narrow strip on the east bank of the Dniester is in the unrecognised breakaway state of Transnistria.

In 1999 Moldova acquired from Ukraine a 0.45 kilometre frontage on the Danube, which turned the village of Giurgiulești into a river port. The name comes from the Moldova River; a legend recounted by the chroniclers Dimitrie Cantemir and Grigore Ureche says that Prince Dragoș named it after his hound Molda, which drowned there.

In antiquity the area was a crossroads for invasions by the Scythians, Goths, Huns and other tribes, followed by periods of Roman and Byzantine control. The Principality of Moldavia emerged in the 1350s, reached prominence under rulers such as Stephen the Great, and was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire from 1538. In 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the eastern half to the Russian Empire, which called it Bessarabia. Southern Bessarabia was returned to Moldavia in 1856, three years before Moldavia united with Wallachia to form Romania, but Russia restored its rule over the entire region in 1878.

Bessarabia declared independence in February 1918 and joined Romania later that year after a vote of its assembly, a decision disputed by Soviet Russia. In 1940, as a consequence of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Romania was compelled to cede Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union, which created the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. It declared independence on 27 August 1991 and took the name Moldova, and the Transnistria War of 1992 left the breakaway region de facto independent.

Moldova adopted its constitution in 1994 and is a parliamentary republic with a 101-seat unicameral parliament. It was granted European Union candidate status in June 2022. The population was an estimated 2,423,300, and ethnic Moldovans were almost 77% of it in the census.
mongolia: Mongolia is a landlocked country between Russia to the north and China to the south, with an area of 1,564,116 square kilometres. Its landscape is grassy steppe, mountains in the north and west, and the Gobi Desert in the south, and the whole country is part of the Mongolian Plateau. The highest point is Khüiten Peak, at 4,374 metres. The climate is high, cold and windy, with long winters, and Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest capital city. The country is subject to harsh conditions known as zud, in which large numbers of livestock die from starvation or freezing.

The Khoit Tsenkher Cave holds paintings dated to 20,000 years ago, and Neolithic agricultural settlements from about 5500 to 3500 BCE predate horse-riding nomadism, which became the dominant culture. The territory was ruled by nomadic empires, among them the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Rouran Khaganate, the First Turkic Khaganate, the Second Turkic Khaganate and the Uyghur Khaganate. In 1206 Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered China proper and established the Yuan dynasty. After the Yuan collapsed, the Mongols retreated to Mongolia and resumed factional conflict, except in the era of Dayan Khan and Tumen Zasagt Khan.

Tibetan Buddhism spread to Mongolia in the 16th century, and by the early 20th century almost one-third of adult men were Buddhist monks. The Qing dynasty absorbed the country in the 17th century. Mongolia declared independence after the Qing collapsed in 1911 and achieved actual independence from the Republic of China in 1921, shortly after which it became a satellite state of the Soviet Union. The Mongolian People's Republic was founded as a socialist state in 1924.

After the anti-communist revolutions of 1989, Mongolia carried out its own peaceful democratic revolution in 1990, which led to a multi-party system, a new constitution in 1992 and a market economy. It is a semi-presidential democratic republic with a unicameral legislature, the State Great Khural, of 126 seats. The 2024 population was 3,544,835, and roughly half live in Ulaanbaatar.
About 30 per cent of the population is nomadic or semi-nomadic, and horse culture remains integral. Mahayana Buddhism is the majority religion, at 51.7 per cent. The traditional dwelling is the ger.
morocco: Morocco has coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, and covers about 446,300 km2. The Atlas Mountains run along the centre and south, the Rif Mountains lie in the north, and both ranges are mainly inhabited by Berber people. Most of the southeast lies in the Sahara Desert and is sparsely populated. The capital is Rabat, beside the Oued Bou Regreg River, and the largest city is the port of Casablanca. The English name Morocco comes from the Spanish Marruecos, itself derived from the name of Marrakesh, the capital of the Almoravid dynasty, the Almohad Caliphate and the Saadian dynasty.

People have lived in the region since the Paleolithic. Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud were dated to roughly 315,000 years ago. At Oued Beht a Neolithic farming society of 3400–2900 BCE formed the largest known agricultural complex in Africa outside the Nile Valley at that time. Phoenicians later established trading colonies, the most substantial being Chellah, Lixus and Mogador.

The Moroccan state traces its origins to the Idrisid dynasty founded by Idris I in 788. It reached its height as a regional power in the 11th and 12th centuries under the Berber Almoravid and Almohad dynasties, which controlled the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the Maghreb. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portugal seized some territory, but the Marinid and Saadi dynasties resisted foreign domination, and Morocco was the only North African nation to escape Ottoman rule. The Alawi dynasty, which still reigns, seized power in 1631. France and Spain established protectorates in 1912, and Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V.

Morocco is a unitary semi-constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament of two chambers, and the 2011 constitutional reforms reduced the king's executive powers and enlarged the prime minister's. The king remains Commander of the Faithful and holds wide powers over the military, foreign policy and religious affairs. The population was about 37 million in the 2024 census. Arabic and Tamazight are the official languages, and Islam is the official religion.
moscow: Moscow lies on the Moskva River, which flows for about 500 kilometres through the East European Plain in Central Russia, and 49 bridges span the river and its canals within the city. The city's name is thought to derive from the river's. The best-grounded theory traces it to a Proto-Balto-Slavic root meaning 'wet', so that Moskva would mean a river at a marsh. A Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, 'Black River'.

The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and around 950 CE two Slavic tribes, the Vyatichi and Krivichi, settled there. Chronicles first mention Moscow in 1147, as a minor town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal and a meeting place for Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich. It was fortified in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built, and was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237–1238 after the destruction of Ryazan.

The Grand Principality of Moscow led the unification of Russian lands in the 15th century, and the Kremlin was rebuilt then, with towers and churches by Italian architects. After the Tsardom of Russia was proclaimed in 1547, Moscow remained its political and economic centre until Peter the Great moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg in 1712, which led to a decline in Moscow's importance through the imperial period. The capital returned to Moscow in 1918, after the establishment of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.

Moscow had 13,010,112 residents in the 2021 census, up from 11,503,501 in 2010. It is a federal city, divided into 12 administrative okrugs and 125 districts. Its road system radiates from the Kremlin and crosses circular roads that began as lines of fortification, among them the Boulevard Ring, on the line of the 16th-century wall of Bely Gorod, and the Garden Ring.

The Moscow Metro opened in 1935, and its original stations were decorated to impress and instruct the population. The city also holds Lomonosov Moscow State University, founded in 1755, and the Tretyakov Gallery, which has works by the icon painter Andrei Rublev.
moskva-river: The river rises about 140 kilometres west of Moscow, crosses Smolensk and Moscow Oblasts and reaches the Oka about 110 kilometres south-east of the capital. Its length is given as 473 kilometres, or by another measure 502, its basin covers 17,600 square kilometres, and it falls 155 metres along its course. An estimated 61 per cent of its water comes from thaw, 12 per cent from rain and 27 per cent from underground sources. It normally freezes around November or December and begins to thaw in late March. On its banks, besides Moscow, stand Mozhaysk, Zvenigorod, Zhukovsky, Bronnitsy and Voskresensk.

Recent studies suggest that the river has occupied its present bed for about 12,000 years. Finnic peoples lived along it, as did Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi. The name of the city is thought to come from that of the river. The most widely accepted explanation derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root connected with wetness, so that it may have meant a river in a marsh or wetland. One Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, black river. To tell the two apart, Russians usually call the river Moskva-reka.

The first stone bridge across it, the Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, was built in 1692. The Vodootvodny Canal, dug in the 1780s, created the island opposite the Kremlin that Muscovites informally call Bolotny Ostrov, Bog Island. Dams built in 1785, 1836 and 1878 failed to keep the river navigable through summer droughts. The highest recorded water level in central Moscow, 127.25 metres above sea level against a usual 120, was reached in the flood of 1908.

Since the Moscow Canal was completed, in 1932–1937, the river has also carried a share of water from the upper Volga, which has made commercial shipping reliable. The average discharge, Volga water included, rises from 38 cubic metres a second near Zvenigorod to 250 at the mouth. As of 2007 there were 49 bridges over the river and its canals within the city, where it is 120 to 200 metres wide and narrowest under the Kremlin walls. Moscow draws its drinking water from five stations on the river and from the upper Volga reservoirs. The stretch within the city freezes only occasionally, on account of contamination.
mozambique: Mozambique lies on the southeast coast of Africa, bordered by the Indian Ocean, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and South Africa. The Zambezi River divides it into two topographical regions. North of the river a narrow coastal strip gives way to inland hills, low plateaus and rugged highlands covered with miombo woodlands.
